# Constitution Making

## By the end of today

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
You will be able to distinguish constitutional politics from ordinary politics and recognize why some American decisions require more than a simple majority.
:::

## Where this fits

Parts 1–3 explained why we limit government.

Part 4: how losers still have a stake in the system.

## Two kinds of politics

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.7em;"}
Constitutional politics sets the rules. Ordinary politics plays inside them.
:::

## Constitutional politics

Near-consensus.

Hard to change.

About the structure of power and the rights that majorities may not touch.

## Ordinary politics

Usually simple majorities.

Taxes, spending, appointments, ordinary statutes.

Winners and losers rotate.

## Why the distinction matters

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
If every election can rewrite the rules, the minority has no reason to stay in the game.
:::

## American ordinary politics is not always 50% + 1

Electoral College.

Senate representation.

Supermajorities for some acts.

Presentment and veto.

## Electoral College

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Presidents are chosen by states as states, not by a single national pool.
:::

That is a constitutional rule, not a glitch in ordinary voting.

## Supermajorities

Treaties: two-thirds of the Senate.

Impeachment conviction: two-thirds of the Senate.

Veto override: two-thirds of both houses.

## Amendments are constitutional politics

![Amendment and contract timeline](../../assets/contract_timeline.jfif){fig-alt="Timeline visual related to constitutional change and the unfinished contract" width="80%"}

Two-thirds of both houses, three-fourths of the states.

## Texas note — easier to amend

The Texas Constitution is long because Texans put ordinary policy into constitutional text.

Easier amendment is a different trade-off: more popular control, less settlement.

## Extra-constitutional institutions

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 1.6em;"}
Some of the hardest brakes are not in the Constitution’s text.
:::

## The filibuster

A Senate practice, not a clause.

It raises the cost of ordinary legislation.

It can be changed by the Senate itself.

## Recap

- Rules-of-the-game politics is supposed to be harder than ordinary politics
- The minority needs a future path to victory and rights after a loss
- Some American “ordinary” institutions already require more than a bare majority
- The filibuster is powerful and optional

## Top Hat

- T/F: Constitutional politics is supposed to be harder to change than ordinary statutes.
- MC: The Electoral College is best classified as:
- Likert: “The Senate filibuster should be treated as if it were part of the written Constitution.”
